title: Judges 18:1–10
context: With the refrain of no king repeated, the tribe of Dan, still without a settled inheritance (compare Joshua 19:47; Judges 1:34), sends five spies north. At Micah’s house they recognize the Levite and ask him for an oracle. They find the quiet, isolated city of Laish and urge their tribe to take it.

verses.text: In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days the tribe of the Danites sought an inheritance to dwell in; for to that day, their inheritance had not fallen to them among the tribes of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The refrain returns, and the Danites seek an inheritance of their own. Arminian readers note that Dan had been allotted land (Joshua 19:40-46) but had not secured it, so the search reflects their failure to possess what God gave.
verses.reformedNotes: Judges 1:34 says the Amorites pressed the Danites into the hill country, and Joshua 19:47 notes that Dan lost territory and took Leshem. Reformed readers see the migration as a consequence of incomplete obedience, framed again by the absence of a king.

verses.text: The children of Dan sent five men of their family from their whole number, men of valor, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to search it. They said to them, “Go, explore the land!” They came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites send five valiant men from Zorah and Eshtaol, Samson’s home region (Judges 13:2, 25). Arminian readers note the echo of the spies sent by Moses and Joshua, now on a mission driven by tribal need rather than God’s command.
verses.reformedNotes: The spies lodge at Micah’s house, linking the two stories. Reformed readers see providence at work in the meeting, even as the people involved act from mixed and largely self-serving motives.

verses.text: When they were by the house of Micah, they knew the voice of the young man the Levite; so they went over there and said to him, “Who brought you here? What do you do in this place? What do you have here?”
verses.arminianNotes: The spies recognize the Levite’s voice and ask who brought him there and what he is doing. Arminian readers hear the questions as pointed: they invite the Levite to examine his calling, though he never does.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the questions expose the irregularity of a Levite serving a private shrine in Ephraim. The narrator uses outsiders to highlight what Israel had ceased to notice.

verses.text: He said to them, “Thus and thus has Micah dealt with me, and he has hired me, and I have become his priest.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Levite says simply that Micah hired him. Arminian readers see the language of hire as revealing: his priesthood rests on a wage, not on God’s call or the people’s need for true worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the Levite describes his office entirely in terms of a human arrangement. Nothing in his answer refers to God, the law, or the tabernacle at Shiloh.

verses.text: They said to him, “Please ask counsel of God, that we may know whether our way which we go shall be prosperous.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Danites ask the Levite to inquire of God about their journey. Arminian readers note the desire for divine approval, sincere perhaps, but sought through an unlawful shrine rather than God’s appointed means.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see people wanting God’s blessing on plans already made. Asking counsel through Micah’s images shows how false worship can still borrow the language of seeking God.

verses.text: The priest said to them, “Go in peace. Your way in which you go is before the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: The priest answers, Go in peace; your way is before the LORD. The reply may mean the LORD watches over them or simply that their way lies open before him, and interpreters note its ambiguity. Arminian readers see a convenient answer that pleases the hearers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the text never says the Levite actually inquired of God. Whatever the oracle meant, the narrator presents it without endorsement, and the later violence at Laish casts doubt on any divine approval.

verses.text: Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in safety, in the way of the Sidonians, quiet and secure; for there was no one in the land possessing authority, that might put them to shame in anything, and they were far from the Sidonians, and had no dealings with anyone else.
verses.arminianNotes: Laish is described as quiet, secure, isolated, and without anyone to shame them. Arminian readers notice the narrator’s sympathetic tone toward a peaceful people, which colors the Danites’ attack that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: The details about Laish’s isolation explain why no one came to its aid (18:28). Reformed readers note that the narrator records the city’s vulnerability without suggesting it deserved destruction, inviting moral reflection on the Danites’ conduct.

verses.text: They came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol; and their brothers asked them, “What do you say?”
verses.arminianNotes: The spies return to their brothers, who ask what they found. Arminian readers note the contrast with the faithful report of Joshua and Caleb, which urged trust in God rather than opportunity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the scene as a parody of the conquest: spies return, a report is given, and the tribe moves, but without a command from God or the presence of the ark.

verses.text: They said, “Arise, and let’s go up against them; for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. Do you stand still? Don’t be slothful to go and to enter in to possess the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The spies say the land is very good and urge the Danites not to be slothful. Arminian readers note the irony that language once used to encourage faith (Numbers 14:7-9) now urges seizing a peaceful city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe how the vocabulary of holy war is borrowed for a tribal raid. The words sound faithful, but the context reveals ambition rather than obedience.

verses.text: When you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people, and the land is large; for God has given it into your hand, a place where there is no lack of anything that is on the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: The spies claim that God has given the land into their hand. Arminian readers caution that invoking God’s name does not prove his approval, and that people often attach divine sanction to their own desires.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a claim of divine gift that the narrator does not confirm. The unsuspecting people and the large land are the real attractions, and the phrase God has given becomes a slogan.
